## Scope and Objectives of the Research

### Novelty of This Research

Building on the TD3/HFT/order-book focus introduced in Chapter I, the novelty
claim here is comparative. A large share of prior RL trading studies target
lower-frequency inputs and evaluate algorithms such as Q-learning, DQN, or PPO
primarily in bar-level settings, whereas this thesis aligns algorithm class,
data granularity, and feature design jointly with high-frequency market
microstructure. This algorithm-data-frequency combination remains less
represented in prior work and defines the core novelty claim tested in the
empirical chapters.

### Hypothesis

The research is based on the following hypotheses, ordered so that each builds on
the previous one; together they make the case that robustness analysis is a
precondition for any credible economic claim:

1. A TD3 agent trained on limit-order-book features learns a risk-adjusted edge
   that survives out of sample. The edge is real but small: it is realised under
   frictionless mid-price execution and is eliminated, not merely eroded, by the
   cost of crossing the spread to trade on it.
2. That edge depends on the assumed transaction cost. It is positive when
   trading is costless and degrades as the per-trade cost rises, with the
   policy ceasing to trade at costs well below the half-spread that must be
   crossed to realise a mid-price edge.
3. A broader state representation improves out-of-sample performance. Replacing
   basic snapshot features with a microstructure-aware feature set raises
   risk-adjusted returns under otherwise identical training and evaluation
   conditions.
4. The reward objective shapes the policy, not only its score. Replacing a
   log-return reward with a Differential Sharpe Ratio reward changes both
   out-of-sample performance and the policy's directional exposure, under
   otherwise identical training and evaluation conditions.

### Objectives of the Research

The study evaluates whether reinforcement learning can extract a tradable
signal from limit-order-book microstructure at tick frequency, and what bounds
that signal economically. The four hypotheses above are tested on one common
apparatus: a TD3 agent trained on six US equities from Nasdaq MBP-10 data,
evaluated out-of-sample against buy-and-hold, TWAP and VWAP execution
benchmarks and a random-action control. DDPG and PPO are trained under the
same configuration, not as claims of their own but so that Hypothesis 1 can be
read as a statement about a learnable signal rather than about one optimizer:
if only TD3 separated from the random control, the edge would be an artefact
of that algorithm rather than a property of the state representation. Significance is assessed against an
economic threshold rather than against zero. At tick frequency each instrument
contributes on the order of a million steps, and a test of the null that the
agent's mean per-step return equals a benchmark's rejects at effect sizes far
below any tradable margin; the question that binds the result is therefore not
whether the difference is distinguishable from zero but whether it exceeds the
cost of trading on it. That is measured directly, by the transaction-cost
sweep in Section 6.2 and the fixed-path bid/ask repricing in Section 7.2.

Each hypothesis is tested as a single-factor comparison. Scenarios differ only in
the quantity under study — the transaction-cost rate for Hypothesis 2, the
feature set for Hypothesis 3, the reward objective for Hypothesis 4 — so that
any difference in out-of-sample performance is attributable to that factor
rather than to an incidental difference in configuration. Hypothesis 1 is
established under frictionless mid-price execution; its economic bound follows
from Hypothesis 2.

Beyond testing the four hypotheses, the study aims to identify which constraint
binds out-of-sample performance: the simplifications in the execution model,
the coverage of the feature set, or the stability of training itself.
Separating these determines which extension is worth pursuing and grounds the
recommendations in Chapter VII.
